title: Did the Resurrection Actually Happen?
excerpt: Everything Christians claim hangs on one event in one weekend, and you are allowed to ask whether it actually happened.
body:
Nobody tells you this when you are young and sitting in a pew. The whole thing rests on one weekend. Not on Jesus being a good teacher. Not on the Sermon on the Mount being beautiful, which it is. The entire structure of Christianity is loaded onto a single claim about a single Sunday morning. A man who was publicly executed, confirmed dead, and sealed in a tomb was alive again two days later. If that did not happen, then Paul himself says the whole thing is a waste of your one short life. He says it plainly. If Christ is not raised, your faith is useless. That is not a guy hedging his bets. That is a man betting everything on a fact.

So you are allowed to ask the question that probably makes the adults around you nervous. Did it actually happen, or is it a comforting story people tell at funerals because the alternative is unbearable. That is not a rebellious question. That is the most reasonable question in the building. The faith itself invites it.

## The Question the Faith Itself Invites

Let me give you the objection in its strongest form, because if I hand you a weak version I am cheating you, and you will spot it. Dead people stay dead. You know this. You have been to a funeral, or you will be. The most universal, most tested, most exceptionless pattern any human being has ever observed is that when someone dies, they do not come back. Every single day, across all of recorded history, the data points the same direction. So when an ancient document claims a resurrection, the smart move is not to investigate, it is to assume the most ordinary explanation, because the most ordinary explanation is almost always the right one. People lie. People hallucinate when they are grieving. Legends grow over decades. Stories get better with each retelling. We know all of these things happen constantly because we watch them happen. We have never once verified a resurrection. So which is more likely. That the laws of biology broke for one Jewish carpenter, or that some heartbroken fishermen and a story got out of hand. Put that way, it sounds like the question answers itself before you even start.

That is the real objection, stated as strongly as I know how. Now let me show you why a lot of serious people, including some who set out to disprove the whole thing, found that the ordinary explanations do not actually hold together when you press on them with any weight.

## The Strongest Form of the Objection

> If Christ is not raised, your faith is useless.

Start with what almost everyone agrees on, because this surprises people. Even scholars who think the resurrection is a myth tend to grant a handful of facts, because the historical evidence for them is strong and granting them does not require believing in miracles. One, Jesus was really crucified by the Romans, who were extremely good at killing people and had no reason to do it halfway. Two, his tomb was found empty by his followers shortly afterward. Three, large numbers of people, individually and in groups, sincerely believed they had seen him alive again. Four, this belief turned a scattered, terrified group of failures into people who would rather die than take it back. These are not church slogans. These are the starting points most historians work from, religious or not. The argument among serious people is not really about these facts. The argument is about the best explanation for the facts. And that is exactly the right way to think about history. You do not prove an event the way you prove a triangle. You weigh the explanations and ask which one accounts for everything at once.

## What Even the Skeptics Concede

So go down the list of ordinary explanations and actually test them, the way you would test an alibi in a courtroom.

## Testing the Ordinary Explanations One by One

Maybe he did not really die. Maybe he just passed out on the cross and woke up later in the cool of the tomb. This one feels clever for about ten seconds, until you remember who did the killing. Roman soldiers executed people for a living. If a prisoner survived, the soldier paid for the mistake with his own life, so they were thorough. They drove a spear into his side specifically to confirm death. And even if you imagine a man surviving a Roman scourging, the crucifixion itself, and a spear wound to the torso, you then have to imagine that same shredded man rolling away a heavy stone from the inside, slipping past a guard, and then walking up to his friends and convincing them not that he needed a doctor, which he obviously would, but that he was the glorious conqueror of death. Nobody starts a world religion limping and bleeding. This theory asks you to swallow something harder to believe than the resurrection it was trying to replace.

Maybe they stole the body. This is the oldest counter theory of them all, and here is the fascinating part. It is recorded right inside the Gospels themselves. Which tells you something. It tells you the empty tomb was not in dispute even by the opponents. Both sides agreed the body was gone. The only argument was about why it was gone. But look hard at what the theft theory actually requires. It requires the disciples to knowingly steal a corpse, knowingly build a lie on top of it, and then knowingly suffer beatings, prison, torture, and execution for that lie, all of them, for the rest of their lives, with not one of them ever cracking under pressure and selling out the others to save his own skin. Think about people you know. People will absolutely die for something they sincerely believe is true. People do not generally die, one by one, in agony, for something they personally know they invented last Tuesday. Liars fold when the cost gets high enough. These men did not fold. The cost got as high as a cost can get, and they did not fold.

Maybe they hallucinated. Grief does strange things to the mind, and people who lose someone they love sometimes feel that person near, even sense them in a room. That is real, and it is gentle to consider. But hallucinations are private events. They happen inside one skull. They do not happen to five hundred people at once, as Paul claims happened, and they do not happen on cue to a hardened skeptic like James, the brother of Jesus, who did not even believe during Jesus' lifetime, or to Paul himself, who was actively on the road to arrest and imprison Christians when it happened to him. A detailed group experience, shared by hundreds, of eating with someone and touching him, is not a recognized psychological event. And there is a harder problem the hallucination theory cannot touch. A hallucination does not empty a tomb. Even if every last follower imagined the whole thing, the body would still have been lying right there in Jerusalem. And the authorities, who badly, desperately wanted this movement crushed, could have ended it in a single afternoon by marching the corpse through the streets. They never did. The simplest reason they never did is that they could not.

Maybe the legend just grew over time, the way fish stories grow with each telling. This is the strongest of the ordinary theories, so give it real respect. Stories do inflate across generations, and we have all watched it happen. But the resurrection claim is not late. The creed Paul quotes in First Corinthians fifteen, the formal list of witnesses, is something scholars across the spectrum, including skeptical ones, date to within just a few years of the crucifixion, possibly within months. That is nowhere near enough time for a legend to bury the facts, especially when the named eyewitnesses are still alive and walking around and could be questioned by anyone who wanted to check. Legends need the witnesses to die off first. These did not have that luxury. N. T. Wright, who has written more carefully on this than almost anyone alive, makes a point that is easy to miss. Nobody in that world was even expecting an individual resurrection in the middle of history. It was not a category their culture had. They believed, if anything, in a general resurrection of everyone at the end of time, not one person rising in the middle of an ordinary week. So they were not primed to invent this. They had no template for it. They had to be confronted with something that forced them to build brand new language to describe it.

## The Witnesses Who Were Not Primed to Invent It

> Nobody starts a world religion limping and bleeding.

Now stack it all up and look at the whole thing at once, because that is where the weight is. The tomb was empty, and the furious enemies of the movement never once produced a body to end it. The witnesses were many and varied, including a skeptic brother and a former persecutor, not just the inner circle who loved him. The followers transformed almost overnight from cowards hiding behind locked doors, terrified of being next, into people who walked into the very same city that had just executed their leader and announced out loud that he was alive, and then refused to stop saying it under threat of death, for decades. Something happened that weekend that turned total defeat into the most stubborn confidence in human history. The question is not whether something happened. Something clearly happened. The question is what is big enough to explain all of it together.

## Stacking the Evidence Together

> The question is not whether something happened.

I am not going to hand you a bow on top of this. Here is the honest part. None of this is a mathematical proof, and anyone who tells you it is, is selling you something, so be careful with them. History does not work like geometry. It works like a courtroom. You weigh the evidence, you look at the alternatives, and you ask what explanation makes the most sense of everything at once. You will always be able to construct some story where it did not happen, the same way a determined person can construct a story where any historical event did not happen. The real question is not whether such a story is possible. It is whether you are believing the more reasonable thing or the less reasonable thing.

What I can tell you is that the lazy version of skepticism, the one that says of course it did not happen, do not even bother looking, is not actually the brave or the smart position. It just feels like it because it is the one in the air around you. The genuinely brave position is to look. To read the alternatives carefully and notice that each one quietly breaks under its own weight when you lean on it. To sit with the strange, stubborn fact that a movement built on a dead leader should have died with him in a week, and instead it outlived the empire that killed him, the empire that eventually bent the knee to the carpenter it had crucified.

## History Works Like a Courtroom, Not Like Geometry

Where to take this. Do not let me, or a youth pastor, or a confident voice on the internet be the last word on something this large. Read someone who argues it carefully and respects your intelligence. Rebecca McLaughlin writes for people exactly your age who are asking exactly this question. N. T. Wright goes much deeper if you want the long version and have the patience for it. And find one adult who will not flinch when you push hard on it, and push on it out loud, to their face. A faith that cannot survive your hardest question was never worth having in the first place. This one has survived sharper questions than yours for two thousand years. It can survive being looked at by you.

title: Can You Actually Trust the Bible?
excerpt: You have heard that the Bible was copied, changed, and voted on by men with an agenda, so here is what the evidence actually shows.
body:
Somebody has probably said it to you already, maybe in a comment section, maybe across a lunch table. The Bible has been copied and recopied and translated so many times that whatever Jesus actually said is long gone, like a game of telephone stretched across two thousand years. By the time it reached you, it is a copy of a copy of a copy of a translation of a forgery. And on top of that, some powerful church officials sat in a room centuries later and voted on which books got in and which got burned, conveniently picking the ones that kept them in charge. So why would you ever hand a book like that your actual life.

That is a fair thing to feel, and I am not going to scold you for feeling it. I want to give you the objection at full strength before I answer it, because you deserve the real version, not a strawman I can knock over with one finger.

## The Telephone Objection at Full Strength

Here is the strongest form. We do not possess a single original document. Not one. Every Bible you have ever held is a translation of copies of copies, and the people doing the copying were human, which means they made mistakes, and at least some of them had reasons to shade things in their own direction. On top of that, the books themselves were written decades after the events by people who already believed, so they are not neutral reporters, they are fans writing about their hero. And then the canon, the official list of which books count, was settled by church councils that had real political power on the line, which means the Bible is not a book that floated down from heaven. It is a committee product. So the whole thing could be unreliable all the way down at the foundation, and you would have no way of knowing.

Now let me walk through it slowly, because almost every single piece of that objection has a real answer, and the answers turn out to be more interesting than the objection itself.

## Why the Copying Was a Family Tree, Not a Single Chain

Start with the telephone problem, because it is the one that sounds most devastating and gets repeated the most. Telephone works as an insult because in the actual game there is only one chain. One person whispers to the next, the message degrades down a single line, and there is no way to check it against anything. But that is simply not how the New Testament was copied. By the second and third centuries, copies were being made in many different places at the same time, in different languages, by communities that did not all know one another and frequently disagreed with one another about important things. So instead of one fragile chain, you get a giant family tree spreading out in every direction across the ancient world. And here is why that completely changes the picture. When you have thousands of copies made independently in scattered places, you can compare them against each other and spot exactly where a scribe slipped, the same way you can catch a typo in your own essay by comparing several drafts. An error introduced by a tired scribe in Egypt does not show up in the copies made in Syria or Rome, so it stands out as the odd one and you can see it for what it is. We are not stuck guessing what got changed. We can reconstruct it.

## The Sheer Weight of the Manuscript Evidence

And the sheer amount of material is the thing that genuinely surprised me when I first looked into it. For most ancient writing, historians are thrilled to have a handful of copies made many centuries after the original. The works of the Roman historian Tacitus survive in very few manuscripts, the earliest copied something like eight hundred years after he wrote, and no serious person stays up at night doubting that Tacitus is roughly what Tacitus wrote. The New Testament, by contrast, survives in thousands of Greek manuscripts, plus thousands more in other ancient languages like Latin and Syriac, with some small fragments dating to within about a hundred years of the writing or even less. If you throw out the New Testament as hopelessly unreliable on manuscript grounds, you have to throw out essentially every other ancient text along with it, because nothing else from that era is even in the same neighborhood for documentation. That is not a Christian talking point. That is just how the documents physically stack up when you line them on a shelf.

## What the Real Differences Actually Are

> A con artist hides the evidence and hopes you do not look.

So what about the changes that real, careful scholars admit do exist. This is where honesty matters, because there genuinely are differences among the manuscripts. Tens of thousands of them, in fact, and that scary number gets thrown around precisely because it sounds enormous. But you have to ask what kind of differences they are. The overwhelming majority are things like a misspelled word, a slip of word order in Greek that does not even change the meaning once you translate it into English, a doubled letter, or an obvious copying hiccup that the comparison method catches instantly. The number of differences that actually affect anything important is tiny, and the ones that do touch something are not hidden from you. Open up almost any decent modern Bible and you will find little footnotes that say things like, some early manuscripts do not include this verse. Stop and think about what that means. The translators are showing you their own work. They are pointing at the seams. They are not papering over the uncertain spots. A con artist hides the evidence and hopes you do not look. These people print the uncertain parts right there in the margin for a fifteen year old to read on a Tuesday. That is the opposite of a cover up. That is a confidence that the text can take the scrutiny.

## The Canon Was Recognized, Not Invented

Now the canon, the committee objection, the picture of men in robes voting on the truth and burning the rejects. The image most people carry, of a single council in a smoky room deciding what God said and torching everything else, is mostly a movie, not history. By the time any council formally listed the books, the core writings, the four Gospels and the letters of Paul, had already been read, copied, quoted, and treated as authoritative by churches scattered across the entire Mediterranean for generations. The councils were not inventing a list out of thin air and imposing it on a surprised church. They were recognizing, and finally writing down, what the wide and far flung community of believers had already been using and trusting for a long time. The rough test was something like this. Did this book trace back to the apostles or their close circle. Was it consistent with the faith that people were already living and dying for. And was it received broadly, across many churches, rather than embraced by one strange splinter group in one city. The books that did not make the cut, the later gospels people love to bring up in arguments, were mostly written much later, by groups with very different ideas about who Jesus was, and they read nothing at all like the earlier material when you actually open them. They were not banned bestsellers ripped from your hands. They were latecomers that the broad church never recognized as theirs in the first place.

## The Embarrassments They Refused to Edit Out

> That roughness is a fingerprint.

Here is the part the telephone insult conveniently forgets to mention. The early Christians had every reason in the world to clean up their own scriptures, and they pointedly did not. If you were inventing a religion and you controlled the editing, you would never leave in the parts where the founder's closest friends look like fools. You would not keep the scene where Peter, the leader, denies even knowing Jesus three separate times in one night to save himself. You would not record that the very first witnesses to the resurrection were women, whose testimony was not even accepted as valid in the courts of that era, which is the last detail on earth you would fabricate if your goal was to convince that particular culture. You would not keep Jesus crying out from the cross that God had forsaken him. Made up propaganda gets sanded down smooth and flattering. These texts are full of splinters and embarrassments and loose ends. That roughness is a fingerprint. It is the fingerprint of people trying hard to preserve what actually happened rather than what would sell well.

## Where This Honestly Leaves You

So where does all of this leave you, honestly. Not at certainty about every single word, and I will not pretend otherwise. The honest position is this. The Bible is far better preserved and far better attested than almost anything else surviving from the ancient world. What it says now is overwhelmingly what it said at the very start. The few genuinely uncertain spots are openly marked for you rather than hidden away. And the books inside it were recognized over time by a wide and frequently divided community rather than dictated by one council with an agenda. That is a strong place to stand. It is not a magic place where doubt becomes illegal and questions get you in trouble. You can trust this book roughly the way you trust the best documented events of ancient history, which is to say a great deal, and still keep asking hard questions about the parts that trouble you.

And there are parts that will trouble you. There are passages that trouble me and have for years. But notice the difference between two separate questions. One question is whether the text reliably reaches you across the centuries, whether you are actually reading what was written. That question has a strong answer, and it is yes. A completely different question is whether you understand and agree with everything the text says once it gets to you. That second one is a lifetime of wrestling, and you are allowed to do both at once, to trust that you have the real words while you struggle with what some of them mean. Do not let anyone rush you past either part.

## Two Different Questions You Must Keep Apart

> Do not let anyone rush you past either part.

Where to take this. If the manuscript stuff grabbed you, read someone who lays it out carefully for normal people rather than scholars. Rebecca McLaughlin and Tim Keller both write about this without burying you under footnotes. If you want to feel the weight of the texts themselves rather than arguments about them, read one whole Gospel straight through in one or two sittings, Mark is the short fast one, and notice for yourself how unpolished and specific and strange it is, how unlike a smooth marketing document. And find someone who actually knows the history, a teacher or pastor or older friend who will not panic or get defensive when you bring up the telephone objection, and bring it to them directly. The answer holds up. It is completely okay to make it prove that it does.

title: If God Is Good, Why Is There So Much Suffering?
excerpt: This is the question that actually drives people away from God, and it deserves far more than a slogan.
body:
This is the one. Not the manuscript stuff, not the science stuff. This is the question that actually empties pews and breaks faith, and it almost never arrives as an argument. It arrives in a hospital room. A kid you know gets sick. A family you love comes apart. You watch the news and see something done to people who did nothing to deserve it. And the words rise up in you before you can stop them. If there is a God, and he is good, and he can do anything at all, then why is this allowed to stand. Why did he not stop it.

I am not going to rush you past that. If anything in this whole series makes you want to throw your phone across the room, it should be the temptation I most have to resist right now, which is the temptation to answer this one quickly and tidily. A fast answer here is a kind of cruelty. So I am going to go slow, and I am going to be honest about where the answers run out.

## Why a Fast Answer Here Is a Kind of Cruelty

Let me state the objection at full strength, the way the philosophers state it, because it is genuinely sharp and it has survived for thousands of years for a reason. It goes like this. If God is all good, he would want to end suffering. If God is all powerful, he would be able to end suffering. And yet suffering is everywhere, and an enormous amount of it appears completely pointless. Therefore, the argument concludes, either God is not all good, or he is not all powerful, or he is not there at all. That is the problem of evil. It is not a trick or a gotcha. It is a real problem, and anyone who tells you it is easy to solve has simply not been paying attention to actual human life.

## The Problem of Evil at Full Strength

Before I say anything constructive, let me clear away the answers that are not good enough, because you have almost certainly been handed some of these, and they did not help, and they may have made things worse.

## Clearing Away the Answers That Are Not Good Enough

Everything happens for a reason, as if there is a tidy purpose stamped neatly on every tumor and every accident. That phrase is not in the Bible. It is a bumper sticker, and it dies the instant you say it to a parent whose child is gone.

They must have done something to deserve it. The Bible actually attacks this one head on, which surprises people. There is an entire book, Job, where a good man suffers horribly and his friends keep insisting he must have secretly earned it somehow, and at the very end God shows up and says the friends were the ones who were wrong, not Job. Jesus does the same thing. When people ask him whose sin caused a particular man to be born blind, he flatly refuses the premise of the question. So if anyone ever tells you that suffering is always a punishment for something, you can tell them, accurately, that the Bible itself disagrees with them.

God will not give you more than you can handle. People say this trying to be kind. It is not true, and it is not actually in there. People get far more than they can handle all the time. Sometimes being given more than you can handle is the entire reason a person finally cries out for help instead of pretending to be fine.

Good. Now that the slogans are off the table, here is where the actual thinking begins.

## Where Your Outrage at Evil Comes From

> Indifferent matter cannot be cruel.

The first thing worth noticing is something C. S. Lewis pointed at, and it is a little sneaky but genuinely important. The moment you call something truly evil, not just unpleasant to you, not just inconvenient, but actually and objectively wrong, you are reaching for a standard of how things ought to be. You are holding the world up against a straight line. But where exactly did you get that line. If the universe is nothing but matter and energy banging around with no purpose behind any of it, then a child suffering is not evil, it is simply an event, in the same way a rockslide or a supernova is an event. Atoms do not commit injustice. Indifferent matter cannot be cruel. The very outrage you feel, the deep sense that this should not be, is a strange and inconvenient thing to be carrying around in a universe that is supposed to be meaningless. Lewis described how his own argument against God had been that the world was so cruel and unjust, and then one day he had to ask himself where on earth he had gotten this idea of just and unjust in the first place. The objection to God quietly borrows a sense of real justice that is very hard to explain without something like God standing behind it. Now, that observation does not make the pain hurt one bit less, and I am not pretending it does. But it does mean the argument is not nearly as one sided as it first appears. The problem of evil cuts in both directions.

## Freedom and the Price of Real Love

> But a world of puppets cannot love, because love that is forced is not love at all, it is just programming.

The second thing to think hard about is freedom. A great deal of the very worst suffering in the world is not weather or disease at all. It is what people deliberately do to one another. And here you have to slow down and really consider what you are actually asking God to do when you ask him to stop it. You want him to stop evil. Fine. But most evil is human choice, so in order to stop it he would have to stop the choosing itself. He would have to reach into every single person in the moment before they do harm and freeze them, override them, turn them into a puppet that can only ever do the kind thing. But a world of puppets cannot love, because love that is forced is not love at all, it is just programming. The same freedom that lets you choose to love your friends, to forgive someone who wronged you, to be brave when it costs you, is the very same freedom that can be turned toward cruelty. You genuinely cannot have the one without the real possibility of the other. A God who made creatures capable of real love necessarily made creatures capable of real damage. That is not a bug in the design. It is the price of the design being love and not control.

Now, an honest person stops me right here and says, fine, that covers the evil that people do to each other, but what about the rest. What about earthquakes. What about cancer in a child. What about the suffering that nobody chose and no human caused. And here I have to be completely straight with you, more straight than a lot of preachers will be. This is exactly where Christianity does not hand you a full explanation, and it does not claim to. The Bible never gives you the master diagram that shows how every particular pain fits neatly into some larger purpose. Job demanded that diagram, demanded it loudly and repeatedly, and God did not give it to him. What God gave Job instead was himself, his own presence, and a long, overwhelming look at how much bigger and stranger and wilder the world is than Job's neat little system of accounting could ever contain. That is not nothing. But it is not the tidy explanation Job asked for either.

And that points straight at the thing that makes the Christian answer different from every other answer human beings have offered, because in the end it is not really an argument at all. It is the cross.

## The Cross, Not an Argument

> The only God there is, in the Christian telling, is the one who has scars on his hands.

Stay with me here, because this is the center of everything. Every other system for dealing with suffering either tells you that suffering is an illusion you need to see through, or it tells you that suffering is simply the way things are so you should toughen up and accept it, or it tells you that you must have earned it somehow. Christianity says something that no other story in the world says. It says that when God finally answered the problem of suffering, he did not do it from a safe distance with a memo or a philosophy lecture. He came down into it personally. The dead center of the entire faith is God himself, in Jesus, being betrayed by a friend, tortured, mocked, and executed in one of the most painful ways humans ever devised. He took the absolute worst that human evil and human suffering could produce and he absorbed it in his own body. Now, whatever you decide to think about that claim, just notice what it does to the question you started with. You can no longer accuse God of not understanding, of watching your pain from a comfortable throne far away while he sips something cold. Tim Keller put it about as well as anyone ever has. We do not know all the reasons God permits the evil and suffering we see. But we do know what the reason is not. It cannot be that he does not love us, or that he does not care, or that he stands aloof from our pain. The cross rules every one of those out forever. The only God there is, in the Christian telling, is the one who has scars on his hands.

## A Promise Backed by an Empty Tomb

And there is one more piece, the part the cross opens up and that you should not miss. The Christian claim is not merely that suffering will eventually be explained to you someday in a debrief. It is that suffering will be defeated, and somehow even undone. The resurrection that follows the cross is the down payment on a promise that the grave does not get the last word. Not that the pain gets erased and pretended away as if it never happened, but that it gets healed so completely and so deeply that, in a strange old phrase, even the bad will somehow become untrue, the way a nightmare becomes untrue the moment you wake up into a bright morning. You are completely allowed to find that hard to believe. But notice what it is and what it is not. It is not a denial of your pain or a request that you minimize it. It is a flat refusal to let your pain be the final word in the sentence.

So here is the honest landing, and there is no bow on it. Christianity does not solve the problem of suffering the way you solve a math problem on a worksheet. If that is what you came here for, no one alive can hand it to you, and you should be deeply suspicious of anyone who claims they can. What it offers instead is stranger, and to a great many people across the centuries, sturdier. A reason your outrage at evil is not just brain chemistry and noise. A reason that real love seems to require real freedom and therefore real risk. A God who did not stay safely out of the pain but walked straight into the deepest part of it. And a promise, backed by an empty tomb, that the whole story is not over yet. That is not a neat resolution. That is a hand to hold onto while you keep asking the question, and you should keep asking it.

Where to take this. If you are in real pain right now, today, do not read another article and do not go looking for the perfect argument. Talk to a person. A trusted adult, a pastor, a counselor, someone who will sit on the floor with you and not try to fix it in one sentence. This question is not finally answered inside your own head. It is answered, as much as it is answered at all, in being known and not left alone. When you are ready for the thinking part, Tim Keller wrote a whole book on exactly this called Walking with God through Pain and Suffering, and C. S. Lewis wrote two, one of them cool and philosophical, and one of them written raw after he lost his wife and could barely stand up. Read the second one. It is brutally honest about how thin all the answers feel when it is finally your turn to suffer. And keep asking your questions out loud. A God who can take the cross can certainly take your anger.

title: Doesn't Science Disprove God?
excerpt: You have been told science and faith are at war, but the history and the actual questions are stranger than the slogan.
body:
You absorbed this one without anyone ever sitting you down to teach it. It is just in the air you breathe. Science is the grownup table, the serious place where you prove things, check them, run them again, and admit it when you turn out to be wrong. Faith is the kids table, the place where you believe stuff because it makes you feel safe and nobody is allowed to ask you for evidence. And the story goes that as science has marched steadily forward, explaining lightning and disease and the origin of the species one by one, it has slowly shoved God out of every hiding place he used to occupy, until now there is basically nothing left for him to do. So the smart, modern, honest thing is to let science have the truth and let religion keep the feelings and the holidays.

Let me give that its strongest form, because I do not want to be soft on it. Science makes testable predictions and then actually checks them against reality, mercilessly, and it has been right about an astonishing number of things. It put human beings on the moon and built the glowing rectangle in your pocket that you would not trade for anything. Religion, the objection says, makes claims that cannot be tested even in principle, and it has a long, embarrassing habit of retreating every single time science finally explains something that used to be a sacred mystery. It used to be that God personally moved the planets across the sky, and then Newton came along and showed it was gravity and math. It used to be that God hand crafted each animal in its present form, and then Darwin showed a mechanism that did not seem to need him. So why on earth would you place your bet on the side that keeps losing ground, decade after decade. Eventually, the argument concludes, God is just a name we give to the shrinking pile of things we have not gotten around to explaining yet.

## The Conflict Thesis at Full Strength

That argument feels strong, and parts of it deserve real respect. Now let me show you the places where it quietly cheats.

Start with the war itself, because the bedrock assumption that science and faith have always been sworn enemies is, ironically, terrible history. The dramatic picture of brave, clear eyed scientists battling against ignorant church goons who hate knowledge and burn books is mostly a story that got invented in the eighteen hundreds by a small number of writers with a specific axe to grind, and historians of science have been quietly dismantling that picture for decades now. Here is the part that should genuinely surprise you and that nobody mentions. Modern science was largely born inside a Christian culture, built in significant part by people who believed in God, and a striking number of them said openly that their faith was the very reason they expected the universe to be understandable in the first place. Sit with that for a second. To do science at all, before you run a single experiment, you have to assume that the universe runs on consistent, rational laws that a human mind is actually capable of grasping. But why would you assume that. If the universe is just random churning matter with nothing behind it, why on earth would you expect it to be orderly, lawful, and elegant enough to write clean equations about. The early scientists had a reason for the assumption built right into their worldview. They believed a rational God had made an orderly world and had given human beings minds capable of reading it. Newton, Kepler, Faraday, Pascal himself, the people who built the whole enterprise from the ground up, were not sneaking science past their faith like contraband. They genuinely thought they were studying the handiwork of a mind. You are free to disagree with their conclusions. But you cannot honestly say that science grew up as the enemy of belief. It grew up, in large part, inside belief's own house, eating at its table.

## The War Itself Is Bad History

> It grew up, in large part, inside belief's own house, eating at its table.

Now the deeper move, and this is the single most important thing I want you to take from this whole article, because it will serve you for the rest of your life and in a hundred conversations. Science and faith are not two rival answers competing to solve the same question. They are answers to fundamentally different kinds of questions, and confusing the two is the exact place where the entire muddle comes from.

## How Questions and Why Questions

Science is spectacularly, world changingly good at answering how questions. How does a cell divide. How did these particular chemicals combine. How does gravity bend space and time. It tells you the mechanism, the process, the unbroken chain of physical causes. What science is simply not built to answer, by its own honest design and the design of every scientist worth the name, is the why and the should and the what for. Take the most loaded example imaginable. Suppose, for the sake of argument, that science one day gives you a complete, flawless, gap free account of how the universe began and how life developed, every single step laid out with no missing pieces. Notice carefully that you still have not touched the questions that actually keep human beings awake at three in the morning. Why is there something rather than nothing at all. Is my life worth anything or not. Is there such a thing as genuine right and wrong, or just things various creatures happen to prefer. Should I be kind even when being kind costs me badly. No experiment in any lab can reach a single one of those. Not because science is weak or failing, but because those are not how questions, and how is the only kind of question its tools can even pick up. A thermometer cannot weigh you. That is not a defect in the thermometer that better engineering will someday fix. It is just not the thing a thermometer is for.

## The Author Behind the Story, Not a Character Inside It

> It is reading another sentence of his book aloud.

Think about a paperback novel sitting on your desk. You could, in principle, give a complete and perfectly true physical account of that book. The exact chemistry of the ink, the wood pulp fibers in the paper, the precise wavelengths of light bouncing off each page into your eye. Every word of that account could be flawlessly accurate. And you would have said exactly nothing about what the story means, whether it is any good, or why it made you cry at the end. The physical description does not compete with the meaning of the story. It runs underneath it, quietly, while the meaning happens at a completely different level. Believers say that God is something like the author standing behind the entire story, not a character squeezed in somewhere inside it competing for elbow room with the other characters. So when science explains a mechanism, it is not crossing God off a list one item at a time. It is reading another sentence of his book aloud. Finding out exactly how the printing press worked does not make the author of the novel vanish into thin air.

## Why the God of the Gaps Is a Bad Bet

That, by the way, is also precisely why the God of the gaps move, the strategy of betting on God to explain whatever science has not figured out yet, is a genuinely bad bet, and honestly believers should stop making it because it keeps blowing up in their faces. If your only reason to believe is the current list of unsolved scientific mysteries, then yes, of course, your faith is going to shrink a little every single time a clever scientist solves one of them. But that was never supposed to be the strong reason. The strong reason was never the gaps in the picture. It was the existence of the picture at all. The brute fact that there is anything whatsoever rather than nothing. That it turned out to be orderly instead of chaotic. That it is beautiful in ways it did not need to be. That you, a clump of atoms, can understand it and ask about it. Those do not shrink when a gap gets filled.

## Fine Tuning and a Universe That Looks Set

> The arrow is not all pointing in one direction.

Which brings me to the one place where the science itself has gotten genuinely strange in a direction worth your attention. It is called fine tuning. Over the last century or so, physicists kept noticing that the basic numbers built into the fabric of the universe, the strength of gravity, the force that holds the nucleus of an atom together, the rate at which the universe expanded in the first instants after it began, all sit within unbelievably narrow ranges. Nudge several of those numbers by a hair in either direction and you do not get a slightly different universe with different scenery. You get no stars, no chemistry, no atoms heavier than hydrogen, no possibility of life anywhere, ever, at all. The settings appear tuned to a precision that is genuinely hard to put into ordinary words. This is not a religious claim being smuggled in. Physicists who believe absolutely nothing about God say it openly, and many of them find it deeply puzzling and want an explanation. There are basically three ways to take it. You can shrug and say it is just a staggering, cosmic accident and leave it there. You can guess that there are countless other universes we cannot see or test, so it is no real surprise that one of them happened to get lucky, though notice that is a very large thing to believe with no evidence you could ever check. Or you can say that it looks tuned because it actually was tuned, by something with intention. Now, fine tuning does not prove God, and I am not going to overplay it the way some eager people do. But notice exactly what it does accomplish. It means that the idea of a mind standing behind the universe is not some embarrassing leftover that science has cornered and is about to finish off. It is a live, serious option that thoughtful scientists, believers and skeptics alike, take seriously and argue about. The arrow is not all pointing in one direction.

## The Honest Landing

So here is the honest landing, with no overclaiming on my part. Science does not disprove God, and it was never built to even try, because the existence of God is not a how question, and how is the only thing science can measure. The famous war between them is mostly a myth invented for other reasons, and the people who actually built science largely did not believe in that war and would have been baffled by it. What science does, magnificently, is describe the intricate machinery of a universe that, the more closely we examine it, looks more surprising and more finely set than anyone ever expected it to. You can look at the whole thing and conclude there is nothing at all behind the curtain. Plenty of brilliant, honest people do exactly that, and you should respect them. But that is not the only intelligent conclusion available, and any person who tells you that science has simply settled the God question and closed the file does not actually understand what science is for or what it can do.

Where to take this. If your real worry underneath all of this is evolution and the opening chapters of Genesis, know that serious, thoughtful Christians hold a genuine range of views on how those two things fit together, and you do not have to pick a final side on it this week or this year. If the fine tuning stuff grabbed you, read someone careful who will not oversell it. Rebecca McLaughlin walks through it for normal people, and there are real working scientists who are also Christians, like Francis Collins, who led the enormous project that mapped the entire human genome, who write directly about exactly this tension from the inside. And do this one concrete thing. The next time someone confidently tells you that science has disproved God, ask them a single, calm question. Which experiment, exactly, was it that tested and disproved it. Then watch what happens to the conversation. The question is far more honest than the slogan it interrupts.

title: Isn't Jesus Just One Way Among Many?
excerpt: Saying one religion is true sounds arrogant in a world of many faiths, so here is why Christians say it anyway and how to say it without sneering.
body:
You have friends. Real ones, not hypothetical ones. Some of them are Muslim, some are Hindu, some have parents who pray in ways your family never has, and some believe absolutely nothing at all and are kinder than half the Christians you happen to know. And then you read a line where Jesus says he is the way, the truth, and the life, and that no one comes to the Father except through him, and something in your stomach tightens up. Because it sounds like he just declared your friends out. It sounds arrogant. It sounds like exactly the kind of claim that has spilled so much blood across so many centuries. And right there, conveniently, sits a quieter and far more decent sounding option. Maybe all the religions are just different paths up the same mountain, all of them reaching toward the same God in their own language and culture, and only a small minded person insists that their particular path is the one and only road to the top.

Let me give that decent sounding option its strongest possible form, because it deserves it and because I find a lot of it genuinely attractive too. Look at the map of the world, the objection says. Whatever religion you happen to have almost certainly lines up neatly with where you were born and who raised you. A kid born in Saudi Arabia is overwhelmingly likely to grow up Muslim. A kid born in much of India is overwhelmingly likely to grow up Hindu. A kid born in your town is statistically likely to end up some flavor of Christian. So if your religion is basically an accident of geography and parentage, how could any one of them possibly be the single true road while all the others are simply wrong. Is it not obviously more humble, more loving, more grown up, to simply say that they are all valid, all sincere, all pointing toward the same ultimate reality in their own way, and to finally stop the ancient, bloody habit of one group insisting it holds the only ticket. From this angle, the exclusive claim itself looks like the actual source of the problem.

## The All Paths Up the Same Mountain Objection

That feels generous and peaceful. Now let me show you why the all paths up the same mountain idea, as genuinely kind as it sounds, does not actually hold together when you look closely, and why it is quietly smuggling in a claim every bit as bold as the one it criticizes.

Start with the mountain image itself, because the entire thing rides on it. To say with confidence that all the religions are climbing the same mountain, you have to be standing somewhere above the mountain, looking down from a height, able to see clearly that all the different paths actually converge at the same summit. You have to somehow know, from that lofty vantage point, what each of the religions is really about underneath all its words and rituals. But stop and ask who handed you that view. The person who confidently says all religions are basically the same has quietly claimed to understand every religion better than its own devoted, lifelong believers understand it. They have to turn to the serious Muslim, the serious Christian, and the serious Buddhist and inform each of them that the thing you think is absolutely essential to your faith is actually not, and that you are all secretly after the very same thing whether you realize it or not. Now notice something. That is not humble at all. That is the single boldest claim in the entire room. It is a claim to a God's eye view that supposedly no human being is allowed to have. Tim Keller makes this point about as sharply as it can be made. The idea that all religions are fundamentally the same is itself an exclusive religious claim, one that most actual religious people firmly reject, and it dresses itself up as neutral and humble when it is neither.

## Who Handed You the View From Above the Mountain

> That is the single boldest claim in the entire room.

And the all the same claim is not even true at the level of plain facts, once you actually read what the religions teach instead of guessing. The major religions do not say the same thing in slightly different accents. They make flatly contradictory claims about the most basic questions a person can ask. Is God personal, a someone who knows your actual name and hears you, or is God an impersonal force or energy, or are there many gods, or is the individual self ultimately an illusion to be dissolved away into the whole. Did Jesus die on a cross, which Christianity treats as the very center and hinge of everything, or did he not die there at all, which Islam states outright and directly. Is your deepest problem sin that needs forgiveness, or ignorance that needs enlightenment, or attachment and desire that need to be extinguished entirely. These are not different scenic routes to the same single summit. They are detailed descriptions of different summits, lying in different directions on the map. To say they are all really the same, you have to firmly ignore what every one of them actually teaches its own people, and that is not respect for those faiths. It is a polite way of not listening to any of them. The genuinely respectful move is to take each faith seriously enough to admit, honestly, that they really do disagree with one another about enormous things.

## The Religions Do Not Actually Say the Same Thing

> They are detailed descriptions of different summits, lying in different directions on the map.

Now back to the geography objection, the one that says your beliefs are just an accident of where you happened to be born. Sit with it, because there is something real and worth keeping in it. It is an excellent reason to hold your own views with humility, to remember constantly that you might easily have grown up believing something entirely different, and to treat every person who believes differently with real respect rather than contempt. Keep all of that. But notice that the argument proves far too much, and that is precisely its fatal weakness as an argument against any belief being true. If where you were born makes your belief untrue or unreliable, then the very same blade swings right back and cuts the confident skeptic in half. A kid raised in a thoroughly secular city, by secular parents, surrounded by secular friends, is statistically very likely indeed to grow up believing there is no God. By the exact logic of the geography objection, that makes atheism just as much an accident of upbringing as anything else. Your beliefs about math probably track closely with where and how you were schooled too. That obvious fact does not make two plus two stop equaling four. Where you happened to first pick up a belief is a completely separate question from whether that belief is actually true. To settle the truth you have to actually examine the belief itself on its merits, not just check the zip code it arrived from. The geography point is a fine and useful warning against arrogance. It is a genuinely terrible argument about what is real.

## What the Geography Objection Really Proves

So why does Christianity make the exclusive claim at all, and can an ordinary person actually make it without turning into an insufferable jerk about it. Here is the heart of the whole thing, and it is not what most people outside expect. The Christian claim is emphatically not that Christians are smarter, or better behaved, or morally superior people who managed to find the one right path by being more clever or more disciplined than everyone else. If anything, it is precisely the reverse. The claim is that human beings could not climb the mountain at all under their own power, that no amount of religious effort or moral striving actually gets anyone to the top, and that this exact helplessness is the entire reason God came down. Look at the structure of it. Nearly every other system in the world is, at bottom, a set of instructions for the climb. Do these things, avoid those things, achieve this inner state, follow this path faithfully, and you will eventually arrive at the summit. Christianity says something startlingly different. It says the actual news is that you cannot make the climb, and that you do not have to, because God himself descended all the way down to exactly where you actually are, in the valley. That descent is what the cross is. So the one way is not a wall built to keep your friends out in the cold. It is a rescue, mounted for people who could not possibly save themselves, a group that very much includes the Christian, who is therefore in absolutely no position to look down on anyone else.

## Why Christianity Makes the Claim at All

And that completely reframes the arrogance worry, if you let it. If a Christian walks around acting superior, smug, like they personally earned something the rest of you missed, then they have badly misunderstood their own faith right down at its root, because the entire point is that nobody earns it and nobody could. A rescued person, pulled half drowned out of the water, does not sneer at the other people still in the water. They point as hard as they can at the boat. The exclusivity, such as it is, lives entirely in the boat, not in the worthiness or cleverness of the passengers who got pulled aboard. So you can genuinely hold that there is one rescue and still treat every single human being you meet as a person of staggering, infinite worth. You can still learn deep things from people of other faiths. You can still freely admit that you have a mountain of things left to learn and that you see only a little. In fact, the same Jesus who said he was the only way was also the one who reached out and touched the people his society had labeled untouchable, who openly praised the faith of foreigners and outsiders over the religious insiders, and who saved his very hardest, most cutting words not for the doubters and the foreigners and the obvious sinners but for the smug religious insiders who were certain they had it all figured out and looked down on everyone else. That is not a recipe for arrogance. That is a constant, stinging rebuke of it, aimed squarely at the religious.

## Rescue Is No Ground for Superiority

> They point as hard as they can at the boat.

So here is the honest landing. The all paths up the same mountain answer feels warm and kind, but it only works by quietly claiming to understand all the religions better than they understand themselves, and by erasing the real and serious and contradictory things they each actually teach, which is not respect for them, it is a gentle way of waving them all off at once. The geography objection is a fine reason for genuine humility and a bad reason to think any particular belief must be false. And the Christian claim that Jesus is the way, once you actually read it in context instead of as a bumper sticker, is not a boast about Christians being the right sort of people. It is a claim that everyone alike needed rescue, and that one came down to get them. You are completely free to reject that claim after you weigh it. But reject the real thing, the actual claim, not the cartoon version of it. And whoever you end up disagreeing with at the end of all your thinking, you are called to treat that person as someone Jesus himself would have walked clear across town to sit down beside.

## Holding It With Both Hands Open

Where to take this. Read the Gospels for yourself, slowly, and watch closely how Jesus actually treats the outsiders, the Samaritan woman at the well, the Roman officer, the people everyone around him had already written off. It is consistently not what you would expect from someone whose message was supposedly about keeping people out. Tim Keller wrote about all of this in The Reason for God, and Rebecca McLaughlin handles the religious diversity question directly and well for younger readers. And then practice the genuinely hard thing out in your real life, with your real friends. Learn to hold what you believe with both hands wide open and both feet planted firmly at the same time, fully convinced and fully kind in the same breath. That particular combination is rare and difficult. It is also, as it turns out, very close to the whole point.

title: It Is Okay to Doubt: What to Do With Your Questions
excerpt: You think your doubts make you a bad Christian, and that fear is doing far more damage than the doubts ever could.
body:
Let me guess at something about you. Somewhere in the last year you had a thought you were afraid to say out loud to anyone. Maybe it was wondering, quietly, whether any of it is actually real. Maybe it was a prayer that seemed to hit the ceiling and bounce right back down to you. Maybe you were sitting in a service feeling like everyone around you was completely sure and you were the only one faking it, and the worst part was not even the doubt itself. The worst part was the second thought that came right behind it, the one that whispered a real Christian would not be thinking this. So you stuffed it down deep where no one could see it. And then it did not go away. It just went underground and quietly got bigger in the dark, the way these things always do.

I want to talk to that. Specifically that. Because in my experience the fear of your doubt is far, far more dangerous to your faith than the doubt itself has ever been or could be.

## The Worry as It Presses at Night

Let me state the worry at full strength, the way it actually sits and presses in your chest at night. If I really believed, the worry says, I simply would not be having these questions. Doubt is the opposite of faith. Faith means being sure, and I am clearly not sure, so maybe I do not actually have it after all. Maybe I am a complete fraud just sitting here in the pew going through the motions. And if I dare to admit any of this out loud to the adults in my church, they will look at me differently forever, or visibly panic, or hand me a single verse with a worried face and change the subject, so I will just keep performing certainty on the outside until I either somehow fake my way into really believing or quietly slip out the back door for good when I am finally old enough to leave.

That is the trap, the whole thing, laid out. And I want to spring it open piece by piece, because almost every single part of it is built on a lie about what faith actually is in the first place.

## The Lie That Faith Means Certainty

Start with the biggest lie holding the whole trap together, the idea that faith means certainty and that doubt is its enemy. This is simply not how the Bible talks about it, not even close. Go open it and look. It is absolutely full of people arguing with God right to his face. The Psalms, which are the songbook of the whole faith, the songs God's own people sang in worship, are loaded with lines like, how long, will you forget me forever, and where are you, and why do you hide. There is a whole psalm that ends sitting in the dark with no resolution at all. Job spends nearly his entire book loudly demanding that God show up and explain himself. There is a man in the Gospels who comes to Jesus and says, in a single breath, I believe, help my unbelief, both things at once, and Jesus does not throw him out for not having enough of one or too much of the other. Jesus helps him on the spot. Even after the resurrection itself, the text flatly says that some of the disciples worshiped and some doubted, standing together in the very same field, looking with their own eyes at the very same risen Jesus. The Bible could so easily have edited that embarrassing detail out. It deliberately left it in. Thomas, the disciple who is famous forever for refusing to believe until he could see and touch the wounds himself, is not condemned and exiled from the group for it. He is personally invited by Jesus to come close and touch. The very book you are so afraid will judge your doubt is, in fact, packed wall to wall with doubters whom God did not throw away.

## Getting the Categories Straight

> The true opposite of faith is indifference, simply not caring enough to even ask the question.

So get the categories straight, because they have almost certainly been scrambled for you somewhere along the way. The true opposite of faith is not doubt. The true opposite of faith is indifference, simply not caring enough to even ask the question. Doubt, real doubt, the kind that keeps you awake and twists in your gut, is not the absence of faith at all. It is faith taking its own questions seriously instead of going numb and checking out. You only ever wrestle with someone you have not yet let go of. The plain fact that this whole thing matters to you so intensely that it actually hurts is not evidence that you are losing your faith. It is evidence that you genuinely have something, something real and worth being torn up about. A person with no faith whatsoever does not lie awake at night wondering whether it might be true. They are not in the room anymore. They left, and they sleep fine.

## Two Different Kinds of Doubt

> Do not bring a careful math answer to a heartache.

Now let me draw you a line that will help you for the rest of your entire life, because not all doubt is the same animal, and treating two very different things as if they were one is a huge part of what makes doubt so terrifying and overwhelming. There is a kind of doubt that is really, underneath, a question. Is the resurrection actually believable as history. How did we even get the Bible and can it be trusted. Why does a good God allow so much suffering. These doubts have real content inside them. They can be looked into and examined. There are entire libraries full of brilliant people who have wrestled hard with each one of them, and you can go and read the arguments on every side and weigh them for yourself. This kind of doubt is not your enemy and never was. It is an assignment. It is your faith asking, politely or not, to finally grow up and have its own reasons instead of just wearing your parents' answers like a borrowed coat. But there is a second kind of doubt that is not really a question at all. It is a mood, or it is a wound. Sometimes you do not actually have any new argument or fresh objection, you are simply exhausted, or someone in the church hurt you badly, or you are anxious about absolutely everything that particular week and God just got swept up into the general fog along with everything else. That kind of doubt is just as real and it matters just as much, but you do not answer it with an argument, because it did not come from one. You answer it the way you answer any deep exhaustion or any wound, with rest, with honesty, with people who love you, and sometimes with real help from a counselor. Knowing which of the two kinds you are actually dealing with at any given moment is honestly half the entire battle. Pascal noticed centuries ago that the heart has its own reasons that the head does not always know anything about, and a great deal of what gets labeled doubt is really the heart talking, not the head. Do not bring a careful math answer to a heartache. It will not fit.

## What to Actually Do With It

Here is the practical part now, what to actually do with all of this, because being told it is okay to doubt is completely useless if nobody ever tells you the next concrete move.

First, say it out loud to an actual person. This is the single hardest one and also by far the most important, and it is the exact thing the trap whispers at you never to do. Doubt grows in secrecy the same way mold grows in a dark, damp closet. The very moment you say the scary thought out loud to a safe human being, it shrinks down to its real size, which is almost always far smaller than the monster it had become inside your own head at two in the morning. Find one adult who will not flinch. Not the one who will obviously panic and start treating you like a problem to be fixed. Not the one who hands you a single verse and immediately changes the subject because you scared them. The one who, when you finally manage to say I am honestly not sure I believe any of this anymore, leans in toward you instead of backing away. Those people genuinely exist, I promise you. A good youth leader. A parent who is honest about their own questions. A pastor actually worth the title. You can test someone with a small doubt first if you need to, to see how they handle it. The right person passes that test, and you will know.

Second, do not make a permanent decision while you are in a temporary state. A great many people walk away from faith for good right in the middle of a season they would not have trusted to pick out their own lunch, let alone settle the largest questions of their existence. Doubt has a way of feeling exactly like clarity. It feels like you have finally, bravely, seen straight through all of it at last. But certainty that arrives suddenly at three in the morning, in either direction, toward belief or away from it, is always a little suspect and worth waiting out. Give your real questions time, and real attention, before you ever let them hand down a final verdict on your whole life.

Third, actually do the work on the question kind of doubt. If your doubt has real content in it, then treat it with the respect it deserves by genuinely investigating it instead of just feeling it over and over on a loop. Go and read the people who took your exact question with total seriousness. C. S. Lewis was a committed atheist who slowly, reluctantly argued his own way in. Lee Strobel was a hard nosed journalist who set out specifically to debunk the whole thing for good and could not do it. Rebecca McLaughlin writes directly for people right around your age who are asking these very things right now, this year. You are absolutely not the first person ever to ask whether the tomb was really empty, or why a good God would allow that much pain. You are joining a very old and very crowded conversation, and that fact should land on you as an enormous relief, not a threat.

## The Honest Landing

> It is not proof that you were never really a believer.

Fourth, keep showing up while you sort it all out, even on the days it feels completely fake. This one sounds backwards, I know, but there is deep wisdom packed inside it. You do not have to feel certain in order to keep praying, keep reading, keep going, keep sitting in the room. An enormous amount of real belief is not a warm feeling you sit around waiting to finally have. It is a thing you keep quietly doing in the dark until, very often, the light comes back from a direction you were not even watching. Remember, the disciples who doubted were standing right there in the field with the ones who worshiped. They had not stormed off. Staying in the room while you wrestle is not hypocrisy. It is patience, and it is a kind of faith all its own.

So here is the honest landing, and it is deliberately not a tidy one, because a tidy one would be a lie. I cannot promise you that if you handle your doubt well and do everything right it will simply dissolve and you will be perfectly sure for the rest of your days. Faith is not a problem you solve once and then file away in a drawer forever. Even people who have believed their whole long lives have their nights. What I can promise you, flat out, is that the doubt is not the disqualification you so deeply fear it is. It is not proof that you were never really a believer. It is, far more often than not, the actual sound of a faith trying to become genuinely your own instead of staying a hand me down coat that never quite fit your shoulders. So the real question was never whether you have doubts. Everyone worth talking to has had them, including the saints, including the people who wrote the book. The real question is what you decide to do with them. Whether you bury them in the dark until they rot and poison everything, or whether you carry them out into the light, to a safe person, to the actual texts and arguments, and ultimately to God himself, who has never once in all of history been afraid of an honest question.

Where to take this. Pick one single person this week, just one, and say one true thing to them about where you actually are right now. That is the entire assignment, nothing more. If you do not yet have that one person in your life, then that lack is itself worth telling someone about. Read Lewis or McLaughlin if your particular doubt has a shape you can name and point at. And if your doubt is all tangled up with a sadness or an anxiety that is plainly bigger than the question itself, then tell a trusted adult that part out loud too, directly, because that is not a faith problem you can read your way out of in a library. That is a weight you were never built to carry alone in the first place. You are not in any trouble for asking. You are standing exactly where a great many of the most serious people of faith have stood before you, in the dark, asking. Keep asking. It is allowed.
